title: What stays the same over time
objectives: Define weak stationarity and judge it from a chart.
Check stationarity with rolling windows and block statistics, and know where the eye fails.

screens.title: Three ways to change
screens.prose: Three seeded series of 500 days, shifted apart so they do not overlap. Each one looks different in its second half from its first, but each in its own way.
screens.question: Match each series to what changes.

tokens.text: How long a move lasts changes

hints.text: For each series compare the first half with the shaded second half.
C keeps the same centre and roughly the same spread. Look at how smooth it is.
A climbs. B swings three times wider after day 250. C wanders in slow waves, then jumps about day to day.

feedback.correct: That's it. A's mean moves, B's variance moves, and C's memory moves.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask of each series in turn: did its centre move, did its spread move, or did its smoothness change?

byKey.level: Look at A again: its centre climbs from about 22 to 32. That is a drifting level.
byKey.spread: Look at B again: its centre stays at 0, but its swings triple after day 250.
byKey.memory: Look at C again: same centre, similar spread, but smooth waves turn into day-to-day noise.

explain.text: Each series breaks one of three promises a stable series keeps: a fixed mean (A), a fixed variance (B), and the same link between days a given gap apart (C). In C's first half, today predicts tomorrow well; in its second half, not at all.

screens.title: Rolling windows
screens.prose: Top: a seeded series that pulls back towards 0. Bottom: a random walk built from the same daily shocks. Each panel shows its rolling mean and rolling sd over the last $w$ days. Slide $w$ from 20 to 260.
screens.question: Which panel's rolling mean and rolling sd stay roughly flat, whatever the window?

options.text: The top panel
The bottom panel
options.why: Slide to 260 and watch the bottom mean: it follows the walk to new levels, and the sd changes with the window.

options.text: Both panels
options.why: The bottom rolling mean moves from about 0 to well below −10. A drifting mean is not flat.

options.text: Neither: every rolling line wobbles
options.why: At $w = 20$ the top lines wobble, but around a fixed centre. Slide to a long window and they settle.

hints.text: Move the slider to 260, then back to 20.
Watch the bottom rolling mean.
The top mean hugs 0 at every window. The bottom mean follows the walk, and its sd grows with the window.

feedback.correct: Correct. The top series keeps a fixed centre and spread; the walk does not.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide the window to its longest and compare the two rolling means.

explain.text: For the top series every window gives a mean near 0 and an sd near 1.15, the series' own values. The walk's rolling mean wanders with it, and its rolling sd is larger the longer the window: a walk's spread depends on how long you look.

screens.title: Weakly stationary
screens.prose: A series is **weakly stationary** when it keeps three promises: a constant mean $E[X_t] = \mu$, a constant variance $\text{Var}(X_t) = \sigma^2$, and $\text{Cov}(X_t, X_{t+k})$ that depends only on the gap $k$. Rolling windows check the first two by eye.

state.caption: Day 3 is the first full window: days 1 to 3.

screens.question: Complete `rolling_mean_sd(x, w)`: trailing windows that end today, NaN until the first window is full, same length as `x`.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np

def rolling_mean_sd(x, w):
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    win = np.lib.stride_tricks.sliding_window_view(x, w)   # row k: x[k], ..., x[k + w - 1]
    pad = np.full(w - 1, np.nan)
    mean = np.concatenate([pad, win.mean(axis=1)])
    sd = np.concatenate([pad, win.std(axis=1, ddof=1)])
    return mean, sd
widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests: the NaN count, the length and the values after the NaNs, rounded to 6 places. One test cuts the series short and expects every earlier value unchanged, since a trailing window cannot see ahead. `make_ar1(phi, n, seed)` and `make_walk(seed, n)` are already defined. The first run loads NumPy, which takes a few seconds.

hints.text: `win.mean(axis=1)` gives one mean per full window.
There are $n - w + 1$ full windows, so $w - 1$ NaNs go in front.
`mean = np.concatenate([pad, win.mean(axis=1)])`, and the same with `win.std(axis=1, ddof=1)`.

feedback.correct: Correct. The cut-short test passed, so no value used a later day.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Put the $w - 1$ NaNs first, then one value per full window.

explain.text: Row $k$ of `win` holds days $k$ to $k + w - 1$, so its mean belongs to day $k + w - 1$: that is why the NaNs go in front. A centred window would use later days and fail the cut-short test.

screens.title: Judging by blocks
screens.prose: Four seeded series of 1,000 days, each cut into four blocks of 250. A chart can fool the eye; block statistics put numbers on it.

state.caption: The first 250 days of the third series.

screens.question: For each series, type yes if its blocks look stationary and no if not.

hints.text: A stationary series has block means close together and block sds close together.
The third series never comes near 0. Is that a problem?
Trend: means climb. Calm then stormy: sds jump. Noise around 5 and the AR(1): both sets of numbers stay put.

feedback.correct: Correct. A mean of 5 is as stationary as a mean of 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look across each row: do the four means agree, and do the four sds agree?

explain.text: Stationary asks whether the mean is constant, not whether it is zero, so noise around 5 passes. The trend fails on its means, the stormy series on its sds. Block numbers turn a judgement by eye into a check you can code.

screens.title: A block check in code
screens.prose: Turn the block judgement into a rule: the block means must lie within `tol` times the series' sd of each other, and so must the block sds. It is a heuristic, not a test: it gives no error rates.
screens.question: Complete `is_roughly_stationary(x, n_blocks, tol)`.

    scale = x.std(ddof=1)

    sds_ok = ...     # range of the block sds within tol * scale

widget.solution:
import numpy as np

def is_roughly_stationary(x, n_blocks, tol):
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    blocks = np.array_split(x, n_blocks)
    means = np.array([b.mean() for b in blocks])
    sds = np.array([b.std(ddof=1) for b in blocks])
    scale = x.std(ddof=1)
    return bool(means.max() - means.min() <= tol * scale and sds.max() - sds.min() <= tol * scale)
widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests on seeded series: white noise, a walk, AR(1) with $\phi = 0.5$ and $0.95$, noise around 5, a variance jump, a trend, and a short list. Each must return True or False as expected. The first run loads NumPy, which takes a few seconds.

hints.text: The range of an array is `a.max() - a.min()`.
White noise passes easily at `tol = 0.5`; the walk fails on its means.
`means_ok = means.max() - means.min() <= tol * scale`, and the same for `sds`.

feedback.correct: Correct. Note the last seeded case: a stationary AR(1) with $\phi = 0.95$ fails the heuristic.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Compare each range with `tol * scale`, for the means and for the sds.

explain.text: The AR(1) with $\phi = 0.95$ is stationary, yet its 250-day blocks disagree: it takes many weeks to forget a shock. A heuristic like this one flags it wrongly, which is why lesson 3 builds a real test.

screens.title: It wanders, so...
screens.prose: Two seeded series of 250 days. One is a stationary AR(1), $x_t = 0.95\,x_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t$. The other is a random walk, $x_t = x_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t$. A colleague says: "The top one wanders far from 0 for months, so it is the walk."
screens.question: What can you conclude from the charts?

options.text: Nothing firm: 250 days of a slow stationary series can look just like a walk
The top one is the walk: it wanders
options.why: You read wandering as a unit root. With $\phi = 0.95$ a shock keeps 60% of its size ten days later, so long excursions are normal. The top one is in fact the AR(1).

options.text: The bottom one is the walk: it drifts away from 0
options.why: That happens to be right, but the chart did not show it. Swap the seeds and the picture can flip.

options.text: Neither is stationary: both leave 0 for long stretches
options.why: You read a long excursion as non-stationary. A stationary series must come back eventually; it need not come back quickly.

hints.text: How long does a shock last when $\phi = 0.95$?
A shock takes about 14 days to halve. In 250 days that leaves room for only a handful of slow swings, which is what a walk shows too.

feedback.correct: Correct. The chart alone cannot settle it. The top one is the stationary AR(1).
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether a slowly reverting series could produce the top chart.

byKey.top: You read wandering as proof of a unit root. The top series is the stationary AR(1); with $\phi = 0.95$ it forgets slowly.
byKey.both: You treated a slow return to 0 as no return. The AR(1) does come back; it just takes weeks.

explain.text: The top series is the AR(1) with $\phi = 0.95$: its range is 18.6 against the walk's 10.4. A shock halves in about $\ln 0.5/\ln 0.95 \approx 14$ days, so 250 days hold only a few swings. The eye cannot separate $\phi = 0.95$ from $\phi = 1$; lesson 3's test tries, with honest error rates.

screens.title: One break
screens.prose: A seeded spread between two share classes: noise around 0 for 250 days, then, after a merger announcement, noise around 4. Each half on its own has a fixed mean and sd.
screens.question: Is the 500-day series stationary?

options.text: No: its mean is 0 before the break and 4 after it
Yes: each half is stationary, so the whole is
options.why: You judged the halves, not the whole. A stationary series has one mean for every day; this one has two.

options.text: Yes: its sd is the same in both halves
options.why: Constant variance is only one of the three promises. The mean breaks the first.

options.text: It depends on which half you are in
options.why: Stationarity is a property of the whole series. Two different means for different days is exactly what it rules out.

hints.text: Is $E[X_t]$ the same for $t = 100$ and $t = 400$?
Look either side of the marker.
Before: mean 0. After: mean 4. One series, two means.

feedback.correct: Correct. Two stationary halves make a non-stationary whole.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first promise, a constant mean, across the whole 500 days.

explain.text: Stationarity needs the same mean for every $t$, so a single break is enough to fail it. A model of the spread fitted before the merger expects 0 and is wrong every day after. Fit each regime separately, or model the break.

screens.title: The variance of an AR(1)
screens.prose: Take $x_t = \phi x_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t$ with $\varepsilon_t$ independent noise of variance $\sigma^2$, independent of the past. If the series is stationary, its variance $\gamma_0$ is the same every day. Find $\gamma_0$.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

hints.text: Start by taking the variance of both sides of the model.
Stationarity is used once, to set $\text{Var}(x_t) = \text{Var}(x_{t-1})$.
Variance of a sum of independent terms, then stationarity, then algebra twice.

feedback.correct: Correct. At $\phi = 1$ the last line divides by 0: a walk has no fixed variance.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take variances first, use stationarity second, then solve.

byKey.d2: Stationarity can only be used once you have a variance equation to apply it to. Take variances first.
byKey.d4: The answer comes last, after collecting the $\gamma_0$ terms.

explain.text: For $\phi = 0.5$ and $\sigma = 1$ this gives $1/0.75 = 1.33$; for $\phi = 0.95$ it gives 10.26. At $\phi = 1$ there is no solution: the walk's variance grows like $t\sigma^2$ instead (Markov Chains, lesson 9).

screens.title: Simulate and check
screens.prose: Now check the formula by simulation. `simulate_ar1(phi, n, seed)` draws $n$ shocks from `np.random.default_rng(seed)`, starts at $x_0 = \varepsilon_0$, and applies $x_t = \phi x_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t$ with $\sigma = 1$.
screens.question: Complete `simulate_ar1` and `variance_of_ar1`.

widget.how: Check runs 9 hidden tests: the first values of seeded paths (rounded to 6 places), a length and the closed form at four values of $\phi$ and $\sigma$. A 20,000-day simulation must also give a variance within 0.05 of the formula. The first run loads NumPy, which takes a few seconds.

hints.text: The loop line is the model itself.
`x[t] = phi * x[t - 1] + e[t]` and `return sigma ** 2 / (1 - phi ** 2)`.

feedback.correct: Correct. 20,000 seeded days with $\phi = 0.5$ give a variance of 1.353, against 1.333.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. The loop applies the model one day at a time; the variance is $\sigma^2/(1 - \phi^2)$.

explain.text: The simulated variance, 1.353, lands close to $1/(1 - 0.25) = 1.333$. Dropping the first 100 days removes most of the start-up from $x_0 = \varepsilon_0$. The closer $\phi$ is to 1, the larger and slower the swings.

screens.title: The definition
screens.prose: You checked three promises. A series is **weakly stationary** when $$E[X_t] = \mu, \qquad \text{Var}(X_t) = \sigma^2, \qquad \text{Cov}(X_t, X_{t+k}) = \gamma_k$$ for every $t$. **Strictly** stationary asks more: the whole joint distribution is unchanged by a shift in time. Fixes: take logs when the spread grows with the level, remove a seasonal pattern, or difference (lesson 4).
screens.question: Which series is weakly stationary?

options.text: Daily white noise with mean 2 and sd 1
A random walk started at 0
options.why: You checked the mean only. A walk's variance is $t\sigma^2$, which grows every day.

options.text: Shop sales with a December peak every year
options.why: You missed the calendar. Its mean depends on the month, so $E[X_t]$ is not constant.

options.text: A price whose daily moves grow as the price grows
options.why: Its variance rises with its level. A log would turn those moves into returns of a steady size.

feedback.correct: Correct. A constant mean of 2 and a constant sd of 1, with no memory at all.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the series that keeps all three promises.

explain.text: White noise keeps all three promises: mean 2, variance 1, and covariance 0 at every gap. The walk breaks the variance promise, the sales the mean promise. A strictly stationary series with a finite variance is also weakly stationary.

screens.title: Before you fit anything
screens.prose: A risk desk fits a volatility model to a fund's daily returns in a calm year. It then uses it through a stormy one. The desk now runs a checklist on every series before fitting, cheapest step first.
screens.question: Put the checklist in order.

lines.text: Plot it: look for trends, breaks and changing swings
Roll it: rolling mean and rolling sd over a few windows
Block it: compare block means and block sds
Test it: run a formal unit-root test (lesson 3)
Fit the model on a series that passed

hints.text: Cheapest first, model last.
The table is step 3; which steps come before it?
Plot, roll, block, test, then fit.

feedback.correct: Correct. Here the sd jumps from 0.60% to 1.96%, so the calm-year model understates the risk by a factor of 3.2.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each step is more formal than the one before it, and the fit comes last.

byKey.fit: You fitted before checking. That is how the calm-year model reached 2020 unchanged.

explain.text: The checklist would have stopped the desk at step 2 or 3: the rolling sd triples halfway through. A model fitted on calm years assumes a variance that the stormy years break. That changing variance is what the GARCH course models.

ideas: Weakly stationary: a constant mean, a constant variance, and a covariance between two days that depends only on the gap between them.
Judge it by eye with a chart and rolling windows, and with block means and sds. Constant does not mean zero: noise around 5 is stationary.
A stationary AR(1) with $\phi$ near 1 wanders for long stretches, so a chart alone cannot tell it from a random walk. Its variance is $\sigma^2/(1 - \phi^2)$.

formula.name: Variance of a stationary AR(1)
formula.note: At $\phi = 1$ there is no fixed variance: a walk spreads like $t\sigma^2$.

summary.trap: "It wanders, so it is not stationary" fails for slow mean reversion: with $\phi = 0.95$, months-long excursions are normal.

quiz.prose: White noise: independent draws with mean 0 and sd 1, one a day.
quiz.question: Is it weakly stationary?

options.text: Yes: constant mean and variance, and zero covariance at every gap
No: a series needs memory to be stationary
options.why: You tied stationarity to memory. White noise has none, and keeps all three promises.

options.text: No: it is too random to be stable
options.why: Stationary describes the distribution, not the path. Every day's distribution is the same.

options.text: Only strictly, not weakly
options.why: Strict stationarity with a finite variance implies weak. White noise is both.

feedback.correct: Correct. White noise is the simplest stationary series.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the three promises one by one.

explain.text: Mean 0 every day, variance 1 every day, and covariance 0 at every gap $k \ge 1$. Stationary, with no memory at all: level 2 of this course calls it pure noise.

quiz.prose: A stationary AR(1) with $\phi = 0.8$ and shock sd $\sigma = 1$.
quiz.question: What is its variance? Give 3 decimal places.

byKey.nosq: You used $1 - \phi$ instead of $1 - \phi^2$. Square $\phi$ first: $1 - 0.64 = 0.36$.
byKey.one: You gave the shock variance. Memory adds to it: each day carries part of the past.

explain.text: $\gamma_0 = 1/(1 - 0.8^2) = 1/0.36 = 2.778$. Memory makes the series swing wider than its daily shocks.

quiz.prose: An analyst has 60 days of a spread. Its rolling mean drifts steadily upward over the whole sample.
quiz.question: What is the safest conclusion?

options.text: The sample is too short to tell drift from a slow swing of a stationary series
The spread is not stationary
options.why: You trusted 60 days. A stationary series with $\phi$ near 1 can climb for 60 days and still come back.

options.text: The spread is stationary because spreads always are
options.why: Some spreads are, many are not. That is what the Cointegration course tests.

options.text: The spread has a deterministic trend
options.why: A steady climb in 60 days is also what a walk or a slow AR(1) produces.

feedback.correct: Correct. Short samples of slow series settle nothing.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how many swings a slow series completes in 60 days.

explain.text: With $\phi = 0.95$ a shock takes about 14 days to halve, so 60 days hold barely one swing. Get more data, or use a test and respect its low power (lesson 3).
